extracted.intended_audience: NSF staff, science policy researchers, program managers, and evaluators studying funding of scientific innovation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodological criteria for conducting a study of scientific innovations and the role of NSF (selection of innovations, measurement of NSF support, investigator interviews, validation, and analytic categories). Intended to produce defensible estimates of NSF's contribution to major advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required study components
rubrics_metrics.description: The study should include at least: (1) a detailed analysis of the issues, starting with those covered in this report, (2) a retrospective look at some major scientific innovations—with emphasis on this century—how they were funded and how they came to be accepted, (3) an assessment of the adequacy of decision-making procedures used by National Science Foundation programs for finding and funding innovative research, and (4) recommendations, if necessary, for modified procedures or new programs designed to ensure that innovative research is funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four numbered elements as the minimal scope for any follow-on evaluation study; each element should be addressed with evidence and recommendations where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'significant innovation'
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts were asked to list 'the most significant innovations since about 1955' including theoretical developments, empirical findings and discoveries, developments in instrumentation, and developments in analytical methods. 'An innovation should be considered significant to the extent that it has contributed to, or itself constitutes, a major conceptual, instrumentational or analytical advance in the field.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rigidly predefine 'significant innovation'—allow expert judgment across these categories, but record the type of innovation (theoretical, empirical, instrumentation, analytical) for later analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert selection and solicitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Designation of significant innovations within each discipline was done by researchers active in the respective fields. The Foundation staff selected this group of scientists based on recommendations from sources such as NSF program staff officers, editors of major journals, and the relevant section of the National Academy of Sciences. About 30 individuals were approached in each of the four fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit roughly 6–10 items per expert, target a mix recommended by program staff, journal editors and academy sections, and make additional contacts as needed to achieve subfield balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use open-ended solicitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The experts were asked an open question that left a major term, 'significant innovation,' undefined. This approach of allowing for increased subjectivity seemed superior to a more limiting questionnaire, and resulted in a wide range of responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer open-ended requests to experts rather than closed questionnaires when attempting to surface candidate innovations, but be prepared for wide variation and the need for subsequent filtering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion rule: require multiple independent mentions
rubrics_metrics.description: In view of the number and mixed nature of advances identified, it was decided to limit the analysis to those innovations mentioned by two or more experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a ‘mentioned by ≥2 experts’ threshold to reduce idiosyncratic items; document the proportion excluded (e.g., 85 of 426 = ~20%) and assess implications for inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validate selection with parallel analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Because such small numbers make statistical inference difficult, a validity check was performed by conducting a parallel analysis of the once-mentioned innovations in chemistry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using a multiple-mention cutoff, run a validation study on single-mention items in at least one field to test for systematic differences between included and excluded items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate expert lists with historical literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehensive review papers (50–100 pages) on significant developments were commissioned to assist in collating and correlating the >1,000 pages describing innovations submitted by practitioners. Sixty-six of the 85 innovations (78 percent) mentioned by two or more panelists were specified in the history papers as significant developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent history/review literature as a check on expert-elicited lists and report overlap percentages as a validity metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify Foundation involvement via grant record search
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant Foundation activity was identified by a review of grant records. All basic research grant files were searched for the names of investigators identified by the outside experts as producers of innovations. The search used computer review for 1968–1976 and specially created files for 1952–1967.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search investigator names across grant files and time windows; document the sources and time periods of records searched and the search methods used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and account for recordkeeping and measurement errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the use of old and existing resources was coupled with a computer search using investigator names, some errors were inevitable. Although results were reviewed and checked by knowledgeable program staff members, it is possible that the results misstate the actuality to some minimal degree. Any such error would be in a conservative direction, however, resulting from the exclusion of grants to investigators due to some quirk of recordkeeping or computer search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify likely error sources (recordkeeping quirks, search limitations) and state probable bias direction (e.g., conservative undercount). Where feasible, perform manual checks or triangulate with other data sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for facility or instrumentation support not visible in project files
rubrics_metrics.description: Another significant source of error could have derived because the research design would not have identified Foundation-financed facilities used in the course of research leading to innovation. In both astronomy and earth sciences, there is some probability that Foundation-financed facilities or instrumentation played a role that would not necessarily be revealed by examining the funding source for the individual project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider facility-level or centralized instrument funding separately; supplement investigator- or project-level grant searches with records of facility investments and instrumentation support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews to establish discovery circumstances and funding sources
rubrics_metrics.description: A telephone survey of the investigators was conducted to obtain information on how the discovery came about—whether the discovery was the intended object or unintended result of the research project—and what sources of funding had been solicited for the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interview principal investigators (or co-investigators where PIs unavailable) and cross-check interview recall against publication acknowledgments and documented funding sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-check interview data against publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of possible problems of recall, the telephone information on sources of support was checked against the source of support reported in the publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat interview responses as one source and verify via contemporaneous publications and grant acknowledgments to reduce recall bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify relationship between project funding rationale and innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews were used to determine whether project funds were solicited with an explicit expectation of the subsequent major advance. Of the 65 projects for which these facts could be determined, only 28 (43 percent) contained in the proposal an explicit and direct reference to the expected advance; 26 (40 percent) were derived from programs for broadly defined research in the general area of the innovation; and 11 (17 percent) were related neither directly nor generally to the justification for the funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use categorical coding: Direct (explicit), General (broad area), Indirect (not related), Not Determined; report percentages and consider implications for peer review's predictive role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count 'instances of support' vs. 'number of innovations'
rubrics_metrics.description: The table reports instances of support for a given innovation. Thus, in astronomy, though there were 21 innovations, 23 instances of support are shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between unique innovations and multiple instances (multiple investigators, multiple supporting grants) when tabulating support; be explicit which numerator is used in percentage calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize patterns of support by field and performing sector
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplines show distinct patterns of support related to overall patterns of research support for the disciplines. For example, astronomy innovations derive overwhelmingly from federally supported projects; industry was a very significant funder of major innovations in chemistry; private foundation support was highly significant in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret NSF contribution relative to field-specific funding ecosystems (industry, foundations, universities, FFRDCs) rather than in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify scope when computing NSF contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: If the foreign and industrial innovation locales are isolated and only NSF's traditional clients (universities, FFRDCs, and Government laboratories) are considered, NSF's contribution to the major advances in each field becomes slightly larger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting NSF share, state whether foreign and industry-based innovations are included or excluded to avoid misleading comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure NSF recognition via prior support to investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on support of investigators rather than on innovations yields a different picture. Defined as investigators who received some NSF support prior to their innovation, NSF's rate of support becomes 44 percent for all investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include measures of prior NSF support to innovators (fellowships, travel grants, facilities) as an indicator of agency recognition and contribution to eventual innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze innovator characteristics (age, team structure, institutional background)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics examined include age at time of innovation (61 percent <35 years), number of investigators per innovation (53 percent created by individuals, 29 percent by pairs, 17 percent by teams of 3+), institutions granting highest degree, and affiliation at time of innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect demographic and collaboration metrics (age distribution, solo vs team, seniority mix, degree institution, employing institution) to understand patterns associated with innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for time-boundedness of judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Table 11.7 illustrates the time-boundedness of judgments about major advances. Judges may be unwilling to make judgments on more recent events, causing low frequencies in recent periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient temporal perspective (avoid labeling very recent work as 'major' prematurely); when analyzing recent periods, note potential undercount due to judge reluctance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use citation analysis cautiously to assess 'good' research
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations in the research literature, when properly qualified, provide a reasonable measure of research quality. However, a citation does not tell what use was made (perfunctory or substantive); each citation must be examined in context to determine the exact kind of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using citation counts or citation utilization studies, qualify interpretations, sample citing contexts, and where possible conduct qualitative checks on the nature of citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up and balance to improve response
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial mailing to experts was followed by reminders. In a few cases, additional individuals were identified and contacted in an effort to achieve balance among subfields within a discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement reminder protocols and add targeted contacts to improve response rates and subfield representation; report response counts and any adjustments made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document unavailable cases and potential biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Some investigators could not be contacted because they were deceased or living abroad; others could not be contacted despite repeated attempts. Note that telephone interviews were conducted for 59 of 85 principal investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report missing data counts, reasons (deceased, abroad, nonresponse), and consider potential bias introduced by uncontactable cases; use alternate informants where possible.
